e-3068.knowledge_point: Finding the Slope of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
e-3068.problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,1,8)$ lies on $C,$ and that $f_y = \dfrac{4x}y - 4x^2y,$ find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
e-3068.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ So, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(2,1,8)$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_y(2,1).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_y(x,y)$ at $(2,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,1) & =\frac{4(2)}{(1)}-4(2)^{2}(1) \\  & =8-16 \\  & =-8\end{aligned}
$$

e-3069.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
e-3069.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\pi.$ Given that the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ lies on $C,$ and that $f_x = y\cos(xy) + \cos y,$ find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
e-3069.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z = f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=\pi.$ So, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x} \Bigg|_{(1,\pi)}.$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\dfrac {\partial z} {\partial x}$ at $(1,\pi)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\pi )} & =\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot \pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi  \\  & =\pi (-1)+(-1) \\  & =-\pi -1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,\pi )} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,\pi )}(x-1) \\ z-(-1) & =(-\pi -1)(x-1) \\ z+1 & =(-\pi -1)x+\pi +1 \\ z & =-(\pi +1)x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

The equation above represents a line in the $xz$-plane. The $xz$-plane through the point $P(1,\pi,-1)$ has the equation $y=\pi.$

So, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\pi,-1)$ is given by the intersection of the following planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\pi  \\ z=-(\pi +1)x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

e-3070.knowledge_point: Finding the Tangent Vector to a Curve at a Point
e-3070.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(0,1,1)$ lies on $C,$ and that $f_x =  \dfrac{\sqrt{2} \pi}{4} \sin{\left(2 x + \dfrac{\pi y}{4} \right)},$ find a tangent vector to $C$ at $P.$
e-3070.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ So, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative $f_x(0,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $f_x(x,y)$ at $(0,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,1) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(0)+\frac{\pi (1)}{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi }{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(0,1) & ={f}_{x}(0,1)(x-0) \\ z-1 & =\frac{\pi }{4}x \\ z & =\frac{\pi }{4}x+1\end{aligned}
$$

The equation above represents a line in the $xz$-plane. The $xz$-plane through the point $P(0,1,1)$ has the equation $y=1.$

So, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0,1,1)$ is given by the intersection of the following planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=\frac{\pi }{4}x+1\end{aligned}
$$

To find a tangent vector, we can find a normal vector to each plane and compute their cross product.

- For the plane $y = 1,$ we write $0x + 1y + 0z = 1$ and find the normal vector $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 0,1,0 \rangle.$

- For the plane $z = \dfrac{\pi}{4} x +1,$ we write $-\dfrac{\pi}{4} x + 0y + 1z = 1$ and find the normal vector $\mathbf{n}_2 = \left\langle -\dfrac{\pi}4,0,1 \right\rangle.$

Computing the cross product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨-\frac{\pi }{4},0,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -\pi /4 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i+\frac{\pi }{4}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we've found a tangent vector, and this could be our final answer. However, just to make our answer a little nicer, we can multiply the vector by $4$ to yield a simpler, parallel vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot (i+\frac{\pi }{4}\,k)=4\,i+\pi \,k\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: A surface $S$ is defined by $z=f(x,y).$ The curve $C$ is the intersection of $S$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Given that the point $P(1,-3,8)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}+y\sqrt{x}$, find the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=-3.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-3,8)$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,-3).$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,-3) & =\frac{{1}^{2}+1}{{1}^{2}(-3)^{2}}+(-3)\sqrt{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}-3(1) \\  & =-\frac{25}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane y=2. Given that the point P(−π2,2,2π) lies on C, and that fx=sin⁡x+xyπ, find the equations of the tangent line to C at P.

a
{y=2z=−2x−π2
b
{y=2z=x−π
c
{y=2z=2x−2π
d
{y=2z=−2x+π
e
{y=2z=x+2π
Submit

decision.explanation: The slope is f_x(-π/2,2)=sin(-π/2)+(-π/2)(2)/π=-2. Point-slope form gives z-2π=-2(x+π/2), so z=-2x+π, with y=2.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=2.$ Given that the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{xy}{\pi }$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{(-\frac{\pi }{2})(2)}{\pi } \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}(x-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\ z-2\pi  & =-2(x+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ z & =-2x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=2 \\ z=-2x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
content.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=2.$ Given that the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\frac{xy}{\pi }$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
content.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{(-\frac{\pi }{2})(2)}{\pi } \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(-\pi /2,2)}(x-(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\ z-2\pi  & =-2(x+\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ z & =-2x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},2,2\pi )$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=2 \\ z=-2x+\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=1. Given that the point P(1,2,4) lies on C, and that fy=3x+y6xy+y2, find the equations of the tangent line to C at P.

a
 {x=2z=−54y+32
b
 {x=1z=−54y+23
c
 {x=1z=45y−32
d
 {x=1z=52y−32
e
 {x=1z=54y+32
Submit

decision.explanation: With x=1 fixed, the slope is f_y(1,2)=(3+2)/√(12+4)=5/4. Thus z-4=(5/4)(y-2), giving x=1 and z=(5/4)y+3/2.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,2,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{6xy+{y}^{2}}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,2,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,2) & =\frac{3(1)+(2)}{\sqrt{6(1)(2)+(2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{16}} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,2)}(y-2) \\ z-4 & =\frac{5}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =\frac{5}{4}y+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,2,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=\frac{5}{4}y+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
content.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,2,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{6xy+{y}^{2}}}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
content.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,2,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,2) & =\frac{3(1)+(2)}{\sqrt{6(1)(2)+(2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{5}{\sqrt{16}} \\  & =\frac{5}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(1,2)}(y-2) \\ z-4 & =\frac{5}{4}(y-2) \\ z & =\frac{5}{4}y+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,2,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=\frac{5}{4}y+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane y=0. Given that the point P(2,0,4) lies on C, and that fx=ey+2xcos⁡y, find the equations of the tangent line to C at P.

a
{x=2z=5y+4
b
{y=0z=5x−14
c
{x=2z=−5x−6
d
{y=0z=5x+6
e
{y=0z=5x−6
Submit

decision.explanation: With y=0 fixed, the slope is f_x(2,0)=e^0+4cos(0)=5. Thus z-4=5(x-2), giving y=0 and z=5x-6.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(2,0,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={e}^{y}+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(2,0,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(2,0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,0) & ={e}^{(0)}+2(2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =1+4 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(2,0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(2,0)}(x-2) \\ z-4 & =5(x-2) \\ z & =5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,0,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
content.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=0.$ Given that the point $P(2,0,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={e}^{y}+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
content.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=0.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(2,0,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(2,0)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,0) & ={e}^{(0)}+2(2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =1+4 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(2,0)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(2,0)}(x-2) \\ z-4 & =5(x-2) \\ z & =5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,0,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=0 \\ z=5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=0.5. Given that the point P(0.5,2,4) lies on C, and that fy=y+2yln⁡(xy)+1x, find the equations of the tangent line to C at P.

a
{x=0.5z=4y−4
b
{x=0.5z=−4y+12
c
{x=0.5z=4y−12
d
{x=0.5z=4x+2
e
{y=2z=4x+2
Submit

decision.explanation: With x=0.5 fixed, the slope is f_y(0.5,2)=2+4ln(1)+2=4. Thus z-4=4(y-2), giving x=0.5 and z=4y-4.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=0.5.$ Given that the point $P(0.5,2,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=y+2y\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\frac{1}{x}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=0.5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(0.5,2,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)}.$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(0.5,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)} & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡((0.5)(2))+\frac{1}{0.5} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: 

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(0.5,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)}(y-2) \\ z-4 & =4(y-2) \\ z & =4y-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0.5,2,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=0.5 \\ z=4y-4\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Tangent Line to a Curve at a Point
content.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=0.5.$ Given that the point $P(0.5,2,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=y+2y\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\frac{1}{x}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
content.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=0.5.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(0.5,2,4)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)}.$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(0.5,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)} & =2+2(2)\operatorname{ln}⁡((0.5)(2))+\frac{1}{0.5} \\  & =2+4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line: 

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(0.5,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(0.5,2)}(y-2) \\ z-4 & =4(y-2) \\ z & =4y-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(0.5,2,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=0.5 \\ z=4y-4\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane y=1. Given that the point P(1,1,0) lies on C, and that fx=3x+6xln⁡(xy), find the equations of the tangent line to C at P.

a
{y=1z=2−2x
b
{y=1,z=4x−4
c
{y=1z=2x−2
d
{y=1z=3x−3
e
{y=1z=3x
Submit

decision.explanation: With y=1 fixed, the slope is f_x(1,1)=3+6ln(1)=3. Through P(1,1,0), the tangent satisfies z=3(x-1)=3x-3 and y=1.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3x+6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(1,1,0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)} & =3(1)+6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1) \\  & =3+6\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(1,1)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1)}(x-1) \\ z-0 & =3(x-1) \\ z & =3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x-3\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the point $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}y)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot 1) \\  & =2\cdot 1-0 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(\frac{\pi }{2},1) & ={f}_{y}(\frac{\pi }{2},1)(y-1) \\ z-0 & =2(y-1) \\ z & =2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(\frac{\pi }{2},1,0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=2y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=2y-2$ (or $2y-z-2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,2,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,2,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+2\,k \\  & =⟨0,1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,1,2⟩.$

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

Question 13
?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=−π2. Given that the point P(−π2,0,2) lies on C, and that fy=sin⁡xcos⁡y2, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
⟨0,0,1⟩
b
⟨0,0,2⟩
c
⟨0,2,1⟩
d
⟨0,2,0⟩
e
⟨0,−2,1⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: With x fixed, f_y(-π/2,0)=sin(-π/2)cos(0)/2=-1/2. A tangent vector is ⟨0,1,-1/2⟩; multiplying by -2 gives ⟨0,-2,1⟩.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Given that the point $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},0,2)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{2}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0) & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{2} \\  & =\frac{(-1)\cdot 1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-\frac{\pi }{2},0) & ={f}_{y}(-\frac{\pi }{2},0)(y-0) \\ z-2 & =-\frac{1}{2}y \\ z & =-\frac{1}{2}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-\frac{\pi }{2},0,2)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ z=-\frac{1}{2}y+2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=-\frac{\pi }{2},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-\frac{1}{2}y+2$ (or $y+2z-4=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,2⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,2⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-2j+k \\  & =⟨0,-2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $⟨0,-2,1⟩.$

Question 13

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=−π2. Given that the point P(−π2,0,2) lies on C, and that fy=sin⁡xcos⁡y2, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
⟨0,0,1⟩
b
⟨0,0,2⟩
c
⟨0,2,1⟩
d
⟨0,2,0⟩
e
⟨0,−2,1⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane x=−π2. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fy(−π2,0).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fy(x,y) at (−π2,0):

fy(−π2,0)=sin⁡(−π2)cos⁡02=(−1)⋅12=−12

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(−π2,0)=fy(−π2,0)(y−0)z−2=−12yz=−12y+2

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(−π2,0,2) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {x=−π2z=−12y+2

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane x=−π2, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨1,0,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=−12y+2 (or y+2z−4=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨0,1,2⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨1,0,0⟩×⟨0,1,2⟩=ijk100012=−2j+k=⟨0,−2,1⟩

Therefore, a tangent vector to C at P is ⟨0,−2,1⟩.

Question 14
?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane y=1. Given that the point P(−1,1,−1) lies on C, and that fx=3ex+y−ln⁡|xy|, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
⟨1,0,−3⟩
b
⟨3,0,1⟩
c
⟨1,0,1⟩
d
⟨1,0,3⟩
e
⟨−1,0,3⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: With y=1 fixed, f_x(-1,1)=3e^0-ln(1)=3. Thus a tangent vector is ⟨1,0,3⟩.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(-1,1,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=3{e}^{x+y}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|xy|$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(-1,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-1,1) & =3{e}^{-1+1}-\operatorname{ln}⁡|(-1)\cdot 1| \\  & =3\cdot 1-\operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\  & =3-0 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-1,1) & ={f}_{x}(-1,1)(x-(-1)) \\ z-(-1) & =3(x+1) \\ z+1 & =3x+3 \\ z & =3x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-1,1,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=3x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=3x+2$ (or $3x-z+2=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨3,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨3,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-3\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-3⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-3⟩=⟨1,0,3⟩$ is also parallel to it.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=1.$ Given that the point $P(2,1,4)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}={e}^{y-1}+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(y-1)$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(2,1).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(2,1) & ={e}^{1-1}+2(2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(1-1) \\  & =1+4 \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(2,1) & ={f}_{x}(2,1)(x-2) \\ z-4 & =5(x-2) \\ z & =5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,1,4)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=1 \\ z=5x-6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=5x-6$ (or $5x-z-6=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨5,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨5,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-5\,k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-5⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-5⟩=⟨1,0,5⟩$ is also parallel to it.
